facts.text: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board investigated the loss of the space shuttle Columbia in 2003; its findings about a computer model used far outside its tested range constitute a case of false confidence from simulation.
facts.quote: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board was the body that investigated the loss of the space shuttle Columbia in 2003

facts.text: During Columbia's launch in January 2003, a piece of insulating foam struck the wing.
facts.quote: During Columbia's launch in January 2003 a piece of insulating foam struck the wing.

facts.text: Engineers assessed Columbia's impact damage using Crater, an empirical model of impact penetration.
facts.quote: Engineers assessed the damage with Crater, an empirical model of impact penetration.

facts.text: The debris that struck Columbia was about 400 times the size of anything in Crater's test database; an early briefing stated 640 times.
facts.quote: The debris was about 400 times the size of anything in the model's test database (an early briefing said 640 times).

facts.text: Crater predicted penetration deeper than Columbia's tile, but engineers overrode the prediction and concluded that the damage would not penetrate because Crater had tended to overpredict in small-impact calibration data and was considered conservative.
facts.quote: Crater actually predicted penetration deeper than the tile, but because the model had tended to overpredict in its small-impact calibration data and was considered conservative, engineers "used their judgment" to conclude the damage would not penetrate

facts.text: Columbia's in-flight damage assessment reported no safety-of-flight issue.
facts.quote: the in-flight assessment reported no safety-of-flight issue.

facts.text: Columbia broke up on re-entry on 1 February 2003.
facts.quote: Columbia broke up on re-entry on 1 February 2003

facts.text: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board reported in August 2003.
facts.quote: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board reported in August 2003.

facts.text: Columbia Accident Investigation Board finding F6.3-10 stated that the damage assessment used an impact simulation well outside Crater's test database.
facts.quote: Finding F6.3-10 said the assessment used "an impact simulation that was well outside Crater's test database"

facts.text: Columbia Accident Investigation Board finding F6.3-10 stated that the analyst performing the damage assessment was inexperienced.
facts.quote: Finding F6.3-10 said the assessment used "an impact simulation that was well outside Crater's test database" and that the analyst was inexperienced

facts.text: Columbia Accident Investigation Board finding F6.3-11 recorded that judgment overrode Crater's prediction.
facts.quote: finding F6.3-11 recorded the override of the model's prediction by judgment.

facts.text: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board criticized briefing slides for burying key information in vague words such as "significant."
facts.quote: The Board also criticized the briefing slides for burying key information in vague words such as "significant"

facts.text: A former shuttle program manager dissented from the false-confidence interpretation of Columbia, arguing that Crater gave a correct warning and management's override caused the failure; the booklet records both views.
facts.quote: A former shuttle program manager has dissented, arguing that Crater gave a correct warning and the failure was management's override of it; the booklet records both views

facts.text: The booklet identifies Columbia as the canonical false-confidence case and concludes that a model's known bias cannot be assumed to hold outside its validated domain; every simulation claim therefore needs an explicit validity envelope and margin.
facts.quote: Columbia is "the canonical false-confidence case", and the lesson is extrapolation: a model's known bias cannot be assumed to hold outside the domain where it was validated, so every simulation claim needs an explicit validity envelope and margin

facts.text: The booklet draws from Columbia the rule that results should be presented in plain charts and words rather than slides that bury caveats.
facts.quote: The booklet also draws from it the rule to present results in plain charts and words rather than slides that bury caveats

facts.text: The Columbia case warns the heavy off-road collision-mitigation program against relying on simulation of machines, sensors and weather that the program has not physically tested.
facts.quote: For a program that will simulate machines, sensors and weather it has not physically tested, the case is a standing warning.
